newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president shakes up team to deflect crisis.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president shakes up team to deflect crisis.

text.p: South Korean president Kim Young-sam on Friday kicked off a sweeping administration reshuffle aimed at restoring his political credibility badly damaged by a loans scandal.
Kim replaced his chief secretary and three other top advisers responsible for political, economic and general affairs, a presidential spokesman said.
"This is the start of a major reshuffle in the government and the ruling party," he said. "The cabinet reshuffle is expected early next week."
Kim Yong-tae, a former home affairs minister who served four terms in parliament, will succeed Kim Kwang-il as chief of staff at the presidential Blue House.

"The new Blue House chief of staff has ample experience in politics and administration and his appointment will contribute to harmony and cooperation among presidential secretaries, the government and the party," the spokesman said.
Kim Yong-tae was once parliamentary leader of the then ruling party under former president Roh Tae-woo.

All members of Kim Young-sam's Blue House inner circle, the entire cabinet and ruling New Korea Party leaders had offered to step down after the president apologised publicly over the scandal on Tuesday, the fourth anniversary of his inauguration.
Kim Young-sam took ultimate responsibility for the loans-for-kickbacks scandal around the failed Hanbo Steel Co although he was not accused of any personal wrongdoing.
The chief Blue House political officer, Lee Won-jong, was replaced by Kang In-sup, a former member of parliament and an ex-journalist.
His counterpart in charge of economic affairs, Lee Suk-chae, stepped down in favour of Kim In-ho, currently head of the Fair Trade Commission.
The president met former finance minister Kim Mahn-je on Thursday, sparking speculation that he would be named as new premier, replacing Lee Soo-sung.
Another person tipped as a candidate for premier is Koh Kun, who held ministerial portfolios for transport, agriculture and home affairs in the 1980s. He is now a university dean.
Domestic media said any new premier was likely to be an economic expert in view of the slowing economy.

South Korea's presidential system concentrates power in the Blue House and Kim's aides have wielded great influence over policy. The chief presidential secretary's job is described by some newspapers as "vice presidency behind the facade".
Political analysts said the president appeared to be fighting to regain his credibility and avoid being labelled a lame duck during his last year in office.

The Hanbo scandal highlighted the failure of President Kim's much-vaunted anti-corruption drive, and he promised on Tuesday to heed criticism that his close associates were incapable of carrying through reforms.
Prosecutors said banks, under pressure from politicians, offered huge loans in return for kickbacks from Hanbo, which piled up $5.8 billion in debts before it was declared insolvent on January 23.

Three of President Kim's senior aides, including a cabinet minister, have been arrested on bribery charges over the scandal. Kim, a former dissident who battled previous military rulers, took power in 1993 vowing a clean society.
Political analysts said the cabinet reshuffle is likely to be announced after the current parliamentary interpellation session ends on Monday.

Hanbo's failure and nearly a month of labour strife caused by the forced passage of a controversial labour law in December have cast gloom over the economy, which grew an estimated 6.9 percent in 1996 against a rise of 9.0 percent in 1995.
